Ryan Greenblatt is lead author of "Alignment faking in LLMs" and one of AI's most productive researchers.

He puts a 25% probability on automating AI research by 2029.

We discuss:

• Concrete evidence for and against AGI coming soon
• The 4 easiest ways for AI to take over
• What evidence we have on how fast / long the intelligence explosion will go
• Would misaligned AGI go rogue early or bide its time
• Whether 'pause at human level' is naive or smart
• Lots more.

My head was often spinning during this interview, in a good way.

Find it on the 80,000 Hours Podcast, links below. Enjoy!

1955390014755377277 [2025-08-12] @danfaggella  [(SEED) type=semantic_search]
Today, Toby Ord's AGI Governance episode is live (the last one was 4+ months ago with YUD himself) today.

He explores the crucial AI and compute trends that are increasing, decreasing, or changing the nature of AGI risk since he published his last book. And yes, we touch on some Successor stuff, too ;)

Some interesting sections that might update your p(doom) and AGI timelines:

00:07:00 - LLMs might have *lessened* our chances of AGI having a kind of near-term "hard takeoff" that humans can't understand. There might be a "kink in the curve" of AGI going beyond human level, because it is so anchored to and reliant on human data.

00:15:37 - We may find that fields where "tastes" is more subjective are areas where AI makes much slower progress. There's a lot of dialogue about "AI research taste" and recursive self-improvement, and toby's takes on this were novel and valuable. 

01:17:37 - Future successors may be "worthy" (have goals and experience as far beyond the richness and depth of our own, as our powers and goals are beyond sea snails), but we really shouldn't *assume* that, and we should be remarkably careful about how we move into a world with systems more powerful than ourselves (Toby gets into some the incentives behind the AGI race here that is different than my take - and I suspect many people will agree with what he thinks is 'driving' lab leaders like Musk and Dario and others).

I hope you enjoy this episode with Toby.

rating.reasoning_summary: This strand represents a static discourse around AGI timelines and forecasting rather than an evolutionary narrative. The boundary object is the question 'When will AGI arrive?' but the conversation remains trapped in prediction mode across 2023-2025. While it includes high-quality artifacts (MacAskill's 'century in a decade' interview, Dwarkesh's continual learning bottleneck thesis), the core idea does not evolve—people simply update their probability distributions without producing new conceptual frameworks or social technologies. The discourse is dialectical (bear vs bull cases) but non-generative: no shared vocabulary emerges, no institutions form, and the community remains in 'wait and see' mode rather than building tools to navigate uncertainty.

essential_tweets.annotation: The seed question establishing the temporal frame (2023 baseline)
Sam Altman's contrarian take: AGI changes less than expected (challenging hype)
MacAskill's 'century in a decade' framework—the closest thing to a boundary object
Yann LeCun's 2022 skepticism aged poorly (evidence of rapid capability gains)
Karpathy's self-driving analogy: warning against hype cycles
Ryan Greenblatt's 25% by 2029 forecast (concrete probability anchoring)
Dwarkesh's bear case video: continual learning as the key bottleneck
Toby Ord on LLMs potentially slowing hard takeoff (late-stage nuance)
